updates.summary: Consensus statement of G20 ministers at the Innovation Ministerial in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, ending 2 September 2026. It presents emerging technologies as drivers of prosperity when 'deployed in a secure and reliable manner', supports sector-specific, risk-based approaches where appropriate and calls on members to preserve national sovereignty in technology governance. Six pillars cover pro-innovation policy, AI in public services, workforce skills, intellectual property policies for AI, 'AI for standards and standards for AI' and supply chains. The Carolina Principles favour secure real-world testing and existing sector-specific regulation, with new rules only for novel issues.

The other deliverables were the G20 AI Prosperity Objectives and the AI Prosperity Compact, on technical workforce development through voluntary partnerships. The UK government published the statement on 4 September 2026. It contains no provisions on frontier-model risks or AI safety institutes.

updates.summary: Statement adopted with the final declaration of the 17th BRICS Summit in Rio de Janeiro. It sets guidelines for AI in the non-military domain: the United Nations at the core of global AI governance, digital sovereignty and each country's right to its own regulatory framework, fair competition, data governance, fair access to AI technology and critical components, copyright protection with transparency over model inputs and outputs, open-source development and inclusive standard-setting. It calls for human oversight, bias mitigation and action against realistic fake content, commits to addressing immediate and long-term risks and malicious use, and calls for a 'prudent approach' to AGI.

It calls for operationalising the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance and the International Independent Scientific Panel on AI. The 2026 New Delhi Declaration (BRICS-02, paragraph 81) commits members to implement it. China's Foreign Ministry published a Chinese text on 9 July 2025.

updates.summary: Call adopted by the G7 Leaders at the Evian summit and supported by Brazil, Egypt, India, Kenya and the Republic of Korea. The leaders recognise risks from children's use of conversational AI systems and ask providers to apply safety settings by default, parental controls and age assurance; remain committed to prohibiting the generation, manipulation and distribution of child sexual abuse material, including deepfakes involving minors, with detection and removal measures by platforms; ask for age-appropriate recommender systems; and call for shared data, impartial evaluations and common assessment standards for AI models and algorithmic systems to evaluate their impact on minors' safety.
updates.notes: Posted on 17 June 2026, the last day of the Evian summit (15 to 17 June 2026). The call welcomes the G7 Common Set of Principles defining a safer and more secure digital space for minors adopted by G7 ministers (supported by the digital ministers on 29 May 2026, G7-04) and asks ministers to meet regularly and assess progress by the end of 2026. It is one of nine statements the Leaders adopted unanimously at Evian; none of the others is on AI: they concern geopolitical issues, cancer, the Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak, international partnerships, critical materials supply chains, growth, migrant smuggling and drug trafficking. A working lunch on 'Ensuring the safe, rapid and effective deployment of artificial intelligence' with partner countries and business leaders took place on 17 June 2026; at the closing press conference President Macron announced work over the following months on a platform for cooperation among democracies on the risks of frontier AI and common standards, with a ministerial meeting planned for September.
